assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches std macro documentation: assert! is always active, debug_assert! is compiled out in release unless debug-assertions are enabled; the guide restates this accurately.
assertions_contracts.evidence: Guide links the std assert documentation itself; semantics unchanged through 1.99.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: assert! for established internal invariants (stays in release), debug_assert! for expensive redundant dev checks, never put required mutation inside an assertion, assertions never replace recoverable input validation.

bounded_work.best_practice: No official Rust source prescribes resource budgets (this is application policy, TigerBeetle/Power-of-Ten lineage); official docs do not contradict it, and std checked_* arithmetic is the documented mechanism the guide uses.
bounded_work.evidence: Stricter than mainstream by design, not contradicted. No 2025-2026 std change removes or deprecates the checked arithmetic APIs relied on.
bounded_work.guide_position: Every loop, queue, retry, allocation and output carries a named bound with units; checked arithmetic before computing ends; explicit stack with depth cap instead of recursion over attacker-controlled depth.

concurrency.best_practice: No official std/async guidance contradicts this; std documents dropping a future as cancellation without guaranteeing started external work stopped, exactly the guide's caution. Tokio (not official) documents the same mutex-across-await hazard.
concurrency.evidence: Guide's async-cancellation section restates documented future-drop semantics accurately; nothing in 1.99 changes the async model.
concurrency.guide_position: Bounded queues with a documented full-queue policy; documented lock ordering and protected invariant; never hold a blocking mutex across .await; own task handles; documented cancellation policy; generation tokens so stale completions cannot publish.

error_handling.best_practice: Current std documentation and idiom agree: Result/Option are the standard mechanisms, ? propagation and structured library errors remain the documented norm; nothing in 1.99 changes this.
error_handling.evidence: Guide cites std assert/Result docs directly; Rust 1.99 release notes contain no error-handling model change.
error_handling.guide_position: Typed errors with bounded context for external/input failures, Option for legitimate absence, ? where the caller owns recovery, explicit match where failure changes cleanup/retry/state, no unwrap/expect on external data, I/O, locks or subprocess results, never silently discard a Result.

formatting.best_practice: rustfmt remains the official formatter shipped with the toolchain; a small shared rustfmt.toml and a 100-column target remain standard practice. The 70-line rule is guide policy, not an official claim, and is labelled as such.
formatting.evidence: No rustfmt deprecation or replacement announced through Rust 1.99; rustfmt still listed among release components/changes.
formatting.guide_position: rustfmt is the mechanical authority; reviewed rustfmt.toml with edition 2024, max_width 100, 4-space tabs; ~70-line function review threshold.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Ownership guidance itself is current, but on the guide's own edition-2024 baseline the unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn lint already warns by default (explicit unsafe blocks inside unsafe fn are the edition default, not an optional extra). Separately, 1.99 std documentation now recommends against reclaiming/deallocating memory obtained via Box::leak and similar leak functions, preferring Box::into_raw/into_non_null patterns - a case the guide never addresses.
memory_ownership.evidence: Edition Guide page for unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn states the lint now warns by default in Rust 2024. Rust 1.99 announcement includes a dedicated section updating Box::leak documentation guidance ahead of custom-allocator stabilization.
memory_ownership.guide_position: Borrow for inspection, own when retaining; clone() as explicit cost; forbid(unsafe_code) default; where unsafe is required, isolate it and 'consider' deny(unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn); local safety docs for every unsafe op; Miri as a gate.

security.best_practice: Aligns with current official guidance (std Command does not invoke a shell on Linux; Child drop does not kill/wait - both restated accurately from std docs). No official source contradicts the stricter positions.
security.evidence: Guide cites std Command and Child documentation directly for the two load-bearing claims; both remain accurate at 1.99.
security.guide_position: forbid(unsafe_code) default; build scripts/proc macros treated as executable trust; lockfile reviewed but not treated as safety proof; Command with separate argv, bounded/drained child output, deadlines, reaping; no secrets in argv or logs; handle-based path policy instead of string prefix checks; TLS verification on.

static_analysis.best_practice: Matches the Cargo/Clippy manual's documented invocation and the Clippy project's own CI guidance; Clippy still ships per-release with the toolchain (1.99 notes link its changelog).
static_analysis.evidence: Guide cites the Cargo manual cargo-clippy page directly; that invocation remains the documented one.
static_analysis.guide_position: Compiler and Clippy warnings actionable, denied in gates (cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings); suppress single lints only at smallest scope with a reason; do not enable every pedantic lint then silence globally; Miri as separate gate for unsafe.

testing.best_practice: Consistent with Cargo book guidance on test organization and profile differences; the debug+release double run is stricter than default practice but not contradicted.
testing.evidence: Gate commands use only documented Cargo/Clippy flags; no flag used by the guide was removed through 1.99.
testing.guide_position: Boundary tests (zero, one, exact limit, limit+1, overflow, cancellation, stale completion, failure before commit), property tests and fuzzing where the input space warrants, hermetic vs external tests separated, feature matrix tested explicitly, gates: fmt check, clippy -D warnings, cargo test debug and release with --locked.

toolchain_pins.best_practice: The pinning mechanism (rustup toolchain files and override rules) is current and correctly described. The recorded baseline is not: current stable is 1.99.0 (2026-10-01), nine releases past the 1.90.0 validation baseline, so the guide's 'tested' evidence no longer describes a current toolchain.
toolchain_pins.evidence: Rust 1.99.0 announcement dated 2026-10-01 on the official blog. rustup override documentation the guide cites is unchanged in substance.
toolchain_pins.guide_position: Pin an exact reviewed nightly date in rust-toolchain.toml (template channel nightly-YYYY-MM-DD, components rustfmt/clippy/rust-src); record active toolchain on disagreement; guide header says 'Document reviewed 2026-09-20' and its validation record says the reference module was compiled with Rust 1.90.0.

current_versions.clippy: Ships as a rustup component versioned with the toolchain (1.99.0); guide's component pin tracks the toolchain
current_versions.debugger: No official Rust debugger; guide pairs the project's pinned toolchain for debugging (lldb/gdb via editor) - no stale named tool found
current_versions.edition: 2024 (current and only new edition; guide baseline matches)
current_versions.miri: Nightly-only component; guide correctly treats it as an optional separate gate when the pinned nightly provides it
current_versions.rust: 1.99.0 stable, released 2026-10-01 (blog.rust-lang.org announcement fetched); next is 1.100, not 2.0
current_versions.rust-analyzer: Official Rust language server (rust-lang/rust-analyzer), distributed as a rustup component; guide names it but its rust-toolchain.toml template component list omits it
current_versions.rustfmt: Ships as a rustup component versioned with the toolchain; max_width 100 is its default target

mechanical_fixes.correct: Re-validate the reference module on the current toolchain (Rust 1.99.0, edition 2024) and record that version, or label 1.90.0 explicitly as a historical validation record
mechanical_fixes.current: compiled with Rust 1.90.0, edition 2024, with warnings denied
mechanical_fixes.evidence: Current stable is Rust 1.99.0, released 2026-10-01; the guide's only recorded compiler validation is nine releases old, so its evidence statement is stale as a current-baseline claim.

mechanical_fixes.correct: State that on edition 2024 unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn already warns by default (explicit unsafe blocks inside unsafe fn are the edition default); present deny as the guide's stricter elevation of that default, not as an optional extra to consider
mechanical_fixes.current:
Instead, isolate the boundary, require review, and consider
`#![deny(unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn)]` to keep unsafe operations visibly scoped.
mechanical_fixes.evidence: The Rust Edition Guide page for this lint states it now warns by default in the 2024 edition, which is the guide's own declared baseline.

proposals.evidence: rust-analyzer is the official Rust language server and is distributed as a rustup component, so it can be pinned in the same file; the guide's template currently cannot deliver its own Section 14 consistency rule.
proposals.proposal: Add rust-analyzer to the rust-toolchain.toml template component list (or state explicitly that it is installed outside the pin). Section 14 requires the project's selected toolchain to drive rust-analyzer, checks, formatting and debugging alike, but the Section 2 template components list contains only rustfmt, clippy and rust-src, so a project copied from the template does not get a pinned rust-analyzer.
proposals.recommendation: Add "rust-analyzer" to the template components and note that per-project opt-out is fine where the editor manages it.

proposals.evidence: Rust 1.99 updated the std documentation for Box::leak to recommend against round-trip unleaking because of interactions with current and future compiler optimizations and the upcoming custom-allocator stabilization, and says the same guidance applies to the other std leak functions.
proposals.proposal: Add a leak rule: memory produced by Box::leak (and the other std leak functions) must not later be reclaimed/deallocated via a round-trip conversion; use Box::into_raw / Box::into_non_null where later reclamation is part of the contract.
proposals.recommendation: Adopt as a one-line ownership rule with an adversarial test on any wrapper that leaks.
